title: Long-tail reuse patterns and memory-channel contention notes
content:
Objective:
- Capture why a small fraction of keys (long tail) are responsible for disproportionate memory bandwidth usage and tail latency during mixed workloads.
- Validate if a stripe-aware eviction policy (evict across memory channel stripes rather than LRU across global address space) reduces memory-channel contention and paging.

Background / motivation:
- Production traces show ~6% of unique keys generate ~48% of cross-node DMA and HBM read bandwidth during peak. Usual LRU eviction clusters evictions into nearby physical pages, amplifying load on a small set of memory channels / PCIe lanes.
- Hypothesis: hot long-tail keys are spatially clustered in the allocator / physical address space, causing channel saturation. Spreading eviction and residency across memory-channel stripes should smooth bandwidth.

Testbed:
- Model: 13B transformer, causal LM, KV cache sharded across 4 GPUs (A100 40GB) per node, NVLink between GPUs, PCIe4 to host.
- Runtime: serving-runtime/sha: a1b2c3d (branch: stripe-evict-proto)
- Workloads: (1) synthetic zipfian request stream (alpha=1.2) with 100k unique keys, (2) sampled production trace (day 2025-10-21) with bursty long-contex requests. Sequence length distribution: median 220, 95p 1500.
- Memory tracing: hw counters (nvidia-smi dmon + nvprof-like sampling), custom kernel-level counters for per-channel HBM read bytes, PCIe read/write bytes, and cross-node DMA.
- Key residency instrumentation: per-key last-access ts, residency-start ts, physical-page hint via jemalloc-physmap.

Experiments run:
1) Baseline: current LRU-ish policy (global recency) + default allocator. 4 runs per workload.
2) Randomized-alloc: same policy but with randomized base virtual-to-physical offset to check allocator influence.
3) Stripe-aware allocator: allocator places KV pages round-robin across 4 HBM/NVLink stripes. Eviction policy modified to prefer evicting keys that free pages on the most-used stripe.
4) Stripe-aware + soft-prefetch: above + small async prefetching for top-100 hot keys at insert.

Key metrics collected (aggregated):
- mean token latency (ms), p95/p99 latency (ms)
- HBM read bandwidth utilization per-channel (GB/s) and imbalance ratio (max/min)%
- PCIe host<->device bandwidth (GB/s) and DMA stalls count
- eviction rate (evictions/sec) and page-reclaim count
- reuse rate: fraction of cache hits that are to keys accessed more than once in a 60s window
- tail miss amplification: number of extra evictions caused by a miss (measured via churn trace)

Results (summary):
- Baseline (prod trace): mean token latency 14.2ms, p95 28.1ms, p99 94.3ms. HBM channel imbalance max/min = 3.7x. PCIe DMA stalls observed 62 instances/5m window correlated with heavy eviction bursts. Reuse rate overall 0.19 (19%).
- Randomized-alloc: small improvement in channel imbalance (3.1x), latency unchanged within noise. Suggests allocator layout contributes but not all of the problem.
- Stripe-aware eviction: mean token latency down to 12.5ms (-12%), p95 24.6ms (-12%), p99 83.2ms (-12%). HBM imbalance reduced to 1.6x (good smoothing). PCIe DMA stalls dropped to 18 instances/5m. Eviction rate roughly same, but page-reclaim events more evenly spread across channels. Reuse rate for hot keys stable (0.21 over top 10% keys).
- Stripe-aware + soft-prefetch: modest further drop in mean latency to 11.9ms; p99 79.7ms. Prefetch increased steady-state HBM usage by ~3% but reduced miss handling spikes. However, prefetching raised overall memory footprint slightly; risk for very memory-constrained nodes.

Observed behaviors and interesting traces:
- Long-tail hotspot example: one key (user-conversation-uuid: abc123) had repeated reinsertions after eviction because its context extension pattern caused accesses every ~3s but LRU placed it behind many one-off short contexts. The key mapped to pages primarily on channel 2, causing periodic channel saturation on bursts.
- Churn amplification: eviction storms often cascade — evicting several keys on same stripe created a short window where multiple subsequent requests all miss and reinsert, creating a feedback loop. Stripe-aware eviction prevents multiple nearby pages from being chosen simultaneously.
- Paging vs reclaim: we saw no OS-level swap, but device-level page-reclaims (GPU memory management) increased tail latency; these were far more frequent when channel imbalance > 2.5x.

Quick notes on instrumentation and caveats:
- jemalloc-physmap is best-effort; virtual->physical mapping on GPU pages is approximate (pinned pages only reliably mapped). Some residual correlation uncertainty exists.
- Workloads used are bursty; longer-running steady workloads show smaller relative improvements since the long tail flattens over time.
- Stripe-aware policy needs allocator support; current prototype only works with contiguous page-size KV backing. Multi-size bucket fills require extra handling (we used 2MB stripe granularity).

Microbench excerpts (trimmed):
- hbm channel reads (baseline run A): [ch0: 48GB/s, ch1: 12GB/s, ch2: 5GB/s, ch3: 13GB/s] => imbalance 9.6x (pathological sample)
- hbm channel reads (stripe-aware run A): [ch0: 28GB/s, ch1: 25GB/s, ch2: 24GB/s, ch3: 23GB/s] => imbalance 1.2x
- eviction churn trace (baseline): spike at t=183s -> 240 evictions/s for 7s correlating with p99 jumps.

Interpretation / short takeaways:
- A small set of keys (long tail) can cause physical-channel hotspots because of allocator and insertion ordering. Classic LRU/clock evictions can exacerbate this by selecting co-located pages.
- Spreading residency across memory-channel stripes significantly reduces channel imbalance and mitigates associated tail latency and DMA stalls.
- Prefetch helps but is only worth it when memory headroom exists; it reduces miss handling spikes but increases background HBM usage.

Next steps / action items:
- (Priya) Flesh out stripe-aware allocator to support variable-sized KV pages (due 2025-11-30). Link PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 (prototype).
- (Liam) Add automated synthetic trace generator that can create configurable spatial locality patterns to stress channels (INF ticket created).
- (Marta) Integrate per-channel throttling metric into Console per-route dashboards (quick win to surface imbalance).
- Evaluate stripe-aware policy under Dedicated reserved capacity shapes and on NVSwitch clusters (different interconnect topology).
- Explore evict-time random jitter across stripe groups to avoid synchronized reinsert storms.

Open questions / experiments to try:
- How does stripe-aware approach interact with quantized KV layouts (4-bit/8-bit packed)? Need to test fragmentation impacts.
- Would a hybrid policy (freq-aware within-stripe but stripe-rotating for global choice) combine best of both worlds?
- Can we detect hot-key spatial clustering online and react by remapping without full migration?

Appendix: commands / scripts used (repo paths trimmed):
- perf-run.sh --trace production-2025-10-21 --policy baseline --out runs/baseline-2025-11-12
- perf-collect.py --run runs/baseline-2025-11-12 --metrics hbm_channels,pci,counters --out runs/summary-baseline.json
- analyze-channel-imbalance.ipynb (quick notebook used to make imbalance plots)

Slack threads / refs:
- #perf-serving: thread "nvlink hotspot after 11/02 deploy" (mentions early symptoms)
- Confluence draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/INF-3421-long-tail-reuse

Notes to self:
- Prototype looks promising for production-ish mixes; prioritize a graceful fallback (disable stripe-awareness) for nodes without allocator support.
- Need to add a micro benchmark to isolate eviction selection cost to ensure stripe-aware doesn't add CPU stalls on heavy insert load.
